source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module A unit 6 (courseware unit 6): controlling

facts.statement: Controlling (courseware): controlling is the last function of the management process, after planning, organising, staffing and directing; it checks whether activities are carried out as planned, measures how far actual performance varies from predetermined benchmarks, investigates the causes of deviation and adjusts accordingly. Characteristics: helps achieve organisational goals; makes the most efficient use of resources; checks the correct application of the standard; builds discipline and order; motivates employees and lifts morale; ensures accurate future planning by re-evaluating standards; improves overall results; reduces errors. Advantages: helps achieve goals, minimises errors, uses resources efficiently, validates the accuracy of standards, improves order and discipline, results in better coordination, simplifies supervision and helps delegation and decentralisation, and supplies feedback for future planning.

Limitations and types of control (courseware): limitations: it may be costly, especially for small firms; it is hard to compare actual performance with standards that are not quantitative (job satisfaction, team spirit, morale); there is little or no control over external factors (government policy, consumer behaviour, technology, competition); employees may resist it as restricting freedom; over-dependence on controls may lead to laxity in supervision; rigid application can slow operations; and wrong controls can expose the organisation to more errors and fraud. Types by timing: feedback control (based on feedback after the activity, so the corrective action can only help similar future activity), proactive control (future-directed, anticipating problems in advance) and concurrent control (real-time, correcting while the activity is carried out).

Control process and planning (courseware): steps: (i) establish goals and standards (communicated clearly; tangible goals such as a sales target of one hundred crore rupees in a year, or intangible ones); (ii) compare actual performance with the predetermined goals and criteria (measure results, seek customer feedback; intangible standards such as market reputation and industrial relations are hard to measure); (iii) take necessary corrective steps promptly when gaps exist; and (iv) continue to monitor the effects of the corrective actions until the problem is solved. Planning and control are inseparable: planning is the foundation of control, control supplies information for later planning, planning comes first and control is the last step, and both look to the future; planning is more evaluative and imaginative while control is more prescriptive and executive.

Traditional control techniques (courseware): personal observation (on-the-spot or direct observation: first-hand information and immediate adjustment, but time-consuming); break-even analysis (cost-volume-profit: the volume at which total revenue equals total cost; break-even point = fixed cost / (price - variable cost); the evaluation uses break-even point, angle of incidence, contribution margin and margin of safety); statistical reports (averages, percentages, coefficient of determination, ratios, shown as charts, graphs and tables); and budgetary control (planning, then comparing actual performance with the budget and acting on deviations; budgets include cash, sales, production, capital and material budgets; a risk is that the budget turns out inaccurate and costly).

Modern control techniques (courseware): return on investment (Du Pont method): ROI = (net income / sales) x (sales / total investment); it can be raised by increasing sales proportionately more than investment or by lowering investment while keeping sales; uses include comparing departments and finding areas with a negative effect. Ratio analysis (profitability, liquidity, solvency and turnover ratios). Responsibility accounting: four responsibility centres (revenue, cost, profit and investment centres). PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) represents the activities of a project in sequence and timing; CPM (Critical Path Method) identifies the tasks necessary for completion and the scheduling flexibility; the critical path is the longest sequence of activities that must be finished on time for the project to be complete. Management information system (MIS): collection of data and management of data. Management audit: examines how a company uses its resources; initiated by top management, may be done at intervals of two or three years, and is not compulsory.

Choosing control techniques (courseware): the choice should consider the character of the company or type of business, the clientele, and the challenges the organisation faces; and factors such as the geographical scope of activities, the management philosophy, the goal of the control, accessibility of methods, associated costs, industry patterns, necessary personnel, time spent and the dependability of the findings.

IT controls (courseware): IT controls aim at confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and the general management of the IT function. Techniques listed: organisational controls (clear responsibilities, job descriptions); management controls (for example an expert committee); financial controls (delegation of financial powers, authorisation, budgetary control, cancellation of documents, dual control, input and output verification, safekeeping, segregation of duties); data processing environment controls; physical access controls; logical access controls (against hacking and viruses); system development life cycle (SDLC) controls; business continuity (BCP) controls (backups and a recovery strategy); and application controls. IT general controls cover the IT environment, change management, source code, SDLC standards, logical access, incident and problem management, technical support, configuration, backup and recovery and physical security. IT application controls (input-processing-output) include completeness, validity, identification, authentication, authorisation and input controls.

COBIT and COSO (courseware): COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology, from the IT Governance Institute) is a framework of best practices for the governance and management of information and technology, with four major domains: planning and organising, acquiring and implementing, delivering and supporting, and monitoring and evaluating. COSO (Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission) identifies five components of internal control: the control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. The CIO or CISO is accountable for the safety, accuracy and dependability of the systems that manage and report the company's data.

payload.title: What controlling is and what it achieves
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Controlling** is the **last function** of the management process. It checks whether work is going **as planned**, measures **how far actual performance differs** from predetermined benchmarks, finds the **causes** of the gap and **adjusts**.

**What it achieves:** it helps **reach goals**, **reduces errors**, makes **efficient use of resources**, **tests whether the standards were right**, builds **order and discipline**, improves **coordination**, **simplifies supervision and delegation**, and gives **feedback for the next plan**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because control compares results against standards, it can also show that a standard was set too high or too low.

self_check.prompt_text: State what the controlling function compares.
self_check.expected_takeaway: It compares actual performance with predetermined standards or benchmarks.

payload.title: Limitations of control
payload.core_explanation_md: **Limits to keep in mind:** control can be **costly**, especially for small firms; it is **hard to apply to non-quantitative standards** such as morale or team spirit; it gives **little control over external factors** (government policy, consumer behaviour, technology, competition); staff may **resist** it as a curb on freedom; **over-reliance** on controls can make supervision lax; **rigid rules slow work**; and **wrong controls** can expose the organisation to more errors and fraud.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These limits show why control must suit the organisation and the activity, not just be applied by habit.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is it hard to control morale?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because morale cannot be measured in quantitative terms against a standard.

payload.title: Three types of control by timing
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Type | When it acts | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feedback control** | After the activity | Helps only **similar future** activity |
| **Concurrent control** | While the activity is carried out | **Immediate**, during the activity |
| **Proactive control** | Before problems arise | **Anticipates** and prevents problems |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A month-end review of last month's variances is feedback control; a supervisor correcting a process on the shop floor is concurrent control; a forecast-based warning before a shortage is proactive control.

self_check.prompt_text: Which control type can only improve similar future activity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Feedback control.

payload.title: The four steps of the control process and its link to planning
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** 1. **Set goals and standards**, clearly communicated (tangible, such as a Rs 100 crore sales target, or intangible). 2. **Compare actual performance** with them; measure results and gather feedback. 3. **Take corrective action promptly** where there are gaps. 4. **Keep monitoring** the effects of the corrective action until the problem is solved.

**Link to planning:** planning is the **foundation and originator** of control; control **returns information** for later planning; planning comes first and control is the **last step**; both look at the **future**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Planning without control cannot show whether plans are being carried out; control without planning has no standards to compare against.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can control not exist without planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because planning sets the objectives and standards against which performance is measured.

payload.title: Break-even point
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **break-even point** is the output at which **total revenue equals total cost**, so there is **neither profit nor loss**.

**In units = fixed cost / (selling price per unit - variable cost per unit)**. The denominator is the **contribution margin per unit**. The **margin of safety** is the part of actual sales **above** the break-even level.

assumptions: Constant price and variable cost per unit
Fixed costs stay fixed over the range
common_errors: Using total cost instead of fixed cost in the numerator
Using price minus total cost per unit in the denominator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware names break-even point, angle of incidence, contribution margin and margin of safety as the measures used; only the first, third and fourth are defined here.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the denominator of the break-even formula?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contribution margin per unit, that is price less variable cost per unit.

payload.title: Traditional techniques: observation, statistical reports and budgets
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Personal observation:** the manager watches work **on the spot**, getting **first-hand information** and correcting at once; it is **time-consuming**.

**Statistical reports:** averages, percentages, ratios and the coefficient of determination, presented as **charts, graphs and tables**, show **areas needing attention**.

**Budgetary control:** plan the budget, **compare actual performance with it** and **act on deviations**. Typical budgets: **cash, sales, production, capital and material**. A risk is that the final budget proves **inaccurate and costly**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Subdividing company goals into departmental budgets makes day-to-day control easier.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two budgets organisations commonly prepare.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the cash budget and the sales budget.

payload.title: Return on investment (Du Pont form)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ROI = (net income / sales) x (sales / total investment)**, the **profit margin** times the **investment turnover**.

ROI rises if **sales grow proportionately more than investment**, or if **investment falls while sales are kept**.

assumptions: Net income, sales and investment are measured over the same period
common_errors: Using profit before tax in one factor and net income in another
Forgetting that sales cancel when the two factors are multiplied

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because sales cancel, ROI equals net income divided by total investment; the two-factor form shows whether margin or turnover is the lever.

self_check.prompt_text: What two ratios multiply to give ROI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Net income over sales and sales over total investment.

payload.title: Ratios, responsibility centres, PERT and CPM, MIS and management audit
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Ratio analysis:** **profitability, liquidity, solvency and turnover** ratios from the financial statements.

**Responsibility accounting:** four centres, **revenue, cost, profit and investment**.

**PERT** shows project activities in **sequence and timing**; **CPM** finds the **tasks needed for completion** and scheduling flexibility; the **critical path** is the **longest** sequence of activities that must finish on time.

**MIS** has two parts, **collection of data** and **management of data**. A **management audit** examines how the company uses its resources, is started by **top management**, may be done every **two or three years** and is **not compulsory**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Selecting among these techniques depends on the type of business, the users and the challenges faced, as well as cost, personnel and the dependability of the findings.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four responsibility centres.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Revenue, cost, profit and investment centres.

payload.title: IT controls
payload.core_explanation_md:
IT controls protect the **confidentiality, integrity and availability** of data and the sound running of the IT function.

**Techniques:** **organisational** (clear responsibilities), **management** (expert committees), **financial** (authorisation, **dual control**, **segregation of duties**, input and output checks), **data processing environment**, **physical access**, **logical access**, **SDLC** and **business continuity** controls.

**IT general controls** cover the IT environment, change management, access, incident handling, backup and recovery. **Application controls** work inside a programme: **completeness, validity, identification, authentication, authorisation and input** controls.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The CIO or CISO is accountable for the safety, accuracy and dependability of the systems that manage and report the company's data.

self_check.prompt_text: What do application controls check that general controls do not?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They check data inside a particular programme from input through processing to output.

payload.title: COBIT and COSO
payload.core_explanation_md:
**COBIT** is a framework of best practice for **governing and managing information and technology**. Its four domains are **planning and organising, acquiring and implementing, delivering and supporting, and monitoring and evaluating**.

**COSO** names five components of internal control: **control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: COBIT is the IT governance framework; COSO is the general internal control framework.

self_check.prompt_text: List the five COSO components.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.

payload.stem_md: A firm has fixed costs of Rs 6,00,000 a year, sells each unit at Rs 150 and has variable cost of Rs 90 per unit. How many units must it sell to break even?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give a whole number of units.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Contribution per unit is 150 - 90 = Rs 60. Break-even = 6,00,000 / 60 = 10,000 units.

payload.stem_md: The same firm actually sells 12,500 units. What is its margin of safety as a percentage of actual sales?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Margin of safety = 12,500 - 10,000 = 2,500 units, which is 2,500 / 12,500 = 20 per cent of actual sales.

worked_solution_steps.description: As a percentage of actual sales.

payload.stem_md: A division has net income of Rs 90 lakh, sales of Rs 900 lakh and total investment of Rs 600 lakh. What is its return on investment by the Du Pont method?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Profit margin = 90 / 900 = 10 per cent; investment turnover = 900 / 600 = 1.5 times; ROI = 10 per cent x 1.5 = 15 per cent.

payload.stem_md: The division cuts its total investment to Rs 500 lakh while sales and net income stay the same. What is the new ROI (per cent, to 1 decimal place)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: ROI = (90 / 900) x (900 / 500) = 0.10 x 1.8 = 18.0 per cent, so reducing investment with sales unchanged raises ROI.

unresolved: This unit is the courseware's account of management control. No regulatory source applies and none was consulted.

Several courseware statements are wrong or loose and were not taught as stated: the break-even point is described as the point where "the purchase price and the selling price are equal" (it is the volume where total revenue equals total cost); the ITGC abbreviation is expanded as "IT Governance Council" in the text although ITGC stands for IT general controls and the list that follows is of general controls; "forensic controls" is given as a category of application controls; and the courseware attributes the break-even evaluation to four measures (break-even point, angle of incidence, contribution margin, margin of safety) without defining angle of incidence. Only the sound content is taught.

The courseware's ROI formula (net income over sales multiplied by sales over total investment) is the Du Pont form and is taught as such. Numbers in the worked and numerical items are invented and are checked in tests/content/batch-abfm-a-u06-b001.test.ts.

items.title: Three types of control by timing
items.core_explanation_md:
| Type | When it acts | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feedback control** | After the activity | Helps only **similar future** activity |
| **Concurrent control** | While the activity is carried out | **Immediate**, during the activity |
| **Proactive control** | Before problems arise | **Anticipates** and prevents problems |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A month-end review of last month's variances is feedback control; a supervisor correcting a process on the shop floor is concurrent control; a forecast-based warning before a shortage is proactive control.

self_check.prompt_text: Which control type can only improve similar future activity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Feedback control.

items.title: The four steps of the control process and its link to planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** 1. **Set goals and standards**, clearly communicated (tangible, such as a Rs 100 crore sales target, or intangible). 2. **Compare actual performance** with them; measure results and gather feedback. 3. **Take corrective action promptly** where there are gaps. 4. **Keep monitoring** the effects of the corrective action until the problem is solved.

**Link to planning:** planning is the **foundation and originator** of control; control **returns information** for later planning; planning comes first and control is the **last step**; both look at the **future**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Planning without control cannot show whether plans are being carried out; control without planning has no standards to compare against.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can control not exist without planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because planning sets the objectives and standards against which performance is measured.

items.title: Break-even point
items.core_explanation_md:
The **break-even point** is the output at which **total revenue equals total cost**, so there is **neither profit nor loss**.

**In units = fixed cost / (selling price per unit - variable cost per unit)**. The denominator is the **contribution margin per unit**. The **margin of safety** is the part of actual sales **above** the break-even level.

assumptions: Constant price and variable cost per unit
Fixed costs stay fixed over the range
common_errors: Using total cost instead of fixed cost in the numerator
Using price minus total cost per unit in the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware names break-even point, angle of incidence, contribution margin and margin of safety as the measures used; only the first, third and fourth are defined here.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the denominator of the break-even formula?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contribution margin per unit, that is price less variable cost per unit.

items.title: Traditional techniques: observation, statistical reports and budgets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Personal observation:** the manager watches work **on the spot**, getting **first-hand information** and correcting at once; it is **time-consuming**.

**Statistical reports:** averages, percentages, ratios and the coefficient of determination, presented as **charts, graphs and tables**, show **areas needing attention**.

**Budgetary control:** plan the budget, **compare actual performance with it** and **act on deviations**. Typical budgets: **cash, sales, production, capital and material**. A risk is that the final budget proves **inaccurate and costly**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Subdividing company goals into departmental budgets makes day-to-day control easier.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two budgets organisations commonly prepare.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the cash budget and the sales budget.

items.title: Return on investment (Du Pont form)
items.core_explanation_md:
**ROI = (net income / sales) x (sales / total investment)**, the **profit margin** times the **investment turnover**.

ROI rises if **sales grow proportionately more than investment**, or if **investment falls while sales are kept**.

assumptions: Net income, sales and investment are measured over the same period
common_errors: Using profit before tax in one factor and net income in another
Forgetting that sales cancel when the two factors are multiplied

items.expanded_explanation_md: Because sales cancel, ROI equals net income divided by total investment; the two-factor form shows whether margin or turnover is the lever.

self_check.prompt_text: What two ratios multiply to give ROI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Net income over sales and sales over total investment.

items.title: Ratios, responsibility centres, PERT and CPM, MIS and management audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ratio analysis:** **profitability, liquidity, solvency and turnover** ratios from the financial statements.

**Responsibility accounting:** four centres, **revenue, cost, profit and investment**.

**PERT** shows project activities in **sequence and timing**; **CPM** finds the **tasks needed for completion** and scheduling flexibility; the **critical path** is the **longest** sequence of activities that must finish on time.

**MIS** has two parts, **collection of data** and **management of data**. A **management audit** examines how the company uses its resources, is started by **top management**, may be done every **two or three years** and is **not compulsory**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Selecting among these techniques depends on the type of business, the users and the challenges faced, as well as cost, personnel and the dependability of the findings.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four responsibility centres.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Revenue, cost, profit and investment centres.

items.title: IT controls
items.core_explanation_md:
IT controls protect the **confidentiality, integrity and availability** of data and the sound running of the IT function.

**Techniques:** **organisational** (clear responsibilities), **management** (expert committees), **financial** (authorisation, **dual control**, **segregation of duties**, input and output checks), **data processing environment**, **physical access**, **logical access**, **SDLC** and **business continuity** controls.

**IT general controls** cover the IT environment, change management, access, incident handling, backup and recovery. **Application controls** work inside a programme: **completeness, validity, identification, authentication, authorisation and input** controls.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The CIO or CISO is accountable for the safety, accuracy and dependability of the systems that manage and report the company's data.

self_check.prompt_text: What do application controls check that general controls do not?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They check data inside a particular programme from input through processing to output.

items.title: COBIT and COSO
items.core_explanation_md:
**COBIT** is a framework of best practice for **governing and managing information and technology**. Its four domains are **planning and organising, acquiring and implementing, delivering and supporting, and monitoring and evaluating**.

**COSO** names five components of internal control: **control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: COBIT is the IT governance framework; COSO is the general internal control framework.

self_check.prompt_text: List the five COSO components.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.

items.stem_md: The division cuts its total investment to Rs 500 lakh while sales and net income stay the same. What is the new ROI (per cent, to 1 decimal place)?
items.correct_explanation_md: ROI = (90 / 900) x (900 / 500) = 0.10 x 1.8 = 18.0 per cent, so reducing investment with sales unchanged raises ROI.
